paragraphs.heading: The middle era
paragraphs.text: The Mesozoic Era ran from about 252 to 66 million years ago and is made up of the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous Periods. It is the middle one of the three eras since complex life evolved, between the Paleozoic and the Cenozoic. Its name, proposed by British geologist John Phillips in 1840, means "middle life", from Greek words for "between" and "living being". It is often called the Age of the Dinosaurs, because dinosaurs were the main land animals for most of it.

paragraphs.heading: Two great extinctions
paragraphs.text: The era began just after the Permian–Triassic extinction, often called the Great Dying because it is seen as the largest mass extinction in Earth's history. Estimates of the marine species lost then run from 90–96% down to as low as 81%. The era ended with the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction, which may have been caused by the asteroid that made Chicxulub Crater on the Yucatán Peninsula, with large volcanic eruptions also thought to have played a part. About half of all genera died out then, including every non-avian dinosaur, along with pterosaurs, mosasaurs and plesiosaurs.

paragraphs.heading: A hot, shifting world
paragraphs.text: During the Mesozoic, the supercontinent Pangaea began breaking into separate landmasses. The climate swung between warmer and cooler spells, but overall Earth was hotter than it is today, with a hot greenhouse climate. Archosaurian reptiles such as the dinosaurs dominated, and the leading plants were gymnosperms such as cycads, ginkgoes and araucarian conifers.

paragraphs.heading: New arrivals
paragraphs.text: The earliest dinosaurs showed up in the Mid-Triassic, and they became the main land vertebrates by the Late Triassic or Early Jurassic, holding that place for about 150 or 135 million years. Archaic birds evolved from a branch of theropod dinosaurs in the Jurassic, and true toothless birds followed in the Cretaceous. The first mammals also arose in this era, but stayed small, under 15 kg, until the Cenozoic. Flowering plants appeared in the Early Cretaceous and spread fast, replacing conifers and other gymnosperms as the main plant group.

paragraphs.heading: The Triassic
paragraphs.text: The Triassic lasted from 251.902 to 201.4 million years ago. Early on, deserts filled the interior of Pangaea, and survivors of the Permian extinction such as Lystrosaurus were the most common land vertebrates. By the Middle Triassic, ecosystems had recovered: corals, sponges and crustaceans came back, and new sea reptiles such as ichthyosaurs evolved. Pangaea began to break up and the Tethys Ocean opened, while reptiles grew larger and the first crocodilians and dinosaurs appeared.

paragraphs.heading: Into the Jurassic
paragraphs.text: The Triassic closed with another mass extinction, the Triassic–Jurassic event, which took most synapsids, almost all large amphibians, many archosaurs and 34% of marine life. Flood basalt eruptions in the Central Atlantic magmatic province are one possible cause. The Jurassic followed, from 201.4 to 143.1 million years ago, and its early climate was tropical and far more humid as large seas opened between landmasses. Plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs and ammonites thrived in the oceans, while theropods such as Dilophosaurus topped the food chain on land. The first true mammals evolved and spread widely while staying fairly small.
